\section{Introduction}

Calkin and Wilf gave a compact explicit enumeration of the positive rational
numbers in \emph{Recounting the Rationals}~\cite{calkinwilf2000}.  The
enumeration is built from the number of hyperbinary representations of a
nonnegative integer.  It has the striking form
\[
  \frac{h(0)}{h(1)},\frac{h(1)}{h(2)},\frac{h(2)}{h(3)},\ldots,
\]
where the consecutive values of $h$ are always relatively prime and every
positive reduced rational occurs exactly once.

The statements below isolate the core theorem and the recurrence lemmas that
make the construction work.  They are phrased so that the central result is the
same enumerating property as in Calkin and Wilf's paper, while leaving the
formal representation of finite sums and finite binary words to the
formalization.

\section{Hyperbinary Representations}

\begin{definition}[Hyperbinary representation]\label{def:hyperbinary_representation}
A hyperbinary representation of a nonnegative integer $n$ is a finite sequence
$(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_k)$ with each
$\varepsilon_i\in\{0,1,2\}$ such that
\[
  n=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\varepsilon_i2^i.
\]
Trailing zeroes are ignored, so two representations that differ only by
extra zeroes at the end are identified.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The hyperbinary counting function]\label{def:hyperbinary_count}
Let $h(n)$ denote the number of hyperbinary representations of $n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Calkin-Wilf fraction]\label{def:calkin_wilf_fraction}
For $n\ge 0$, define
\[
  q_n=\frac{h(n)}{h(n+1)}.
\]
\end{definition}

\section{Recurrences}

\begin{lemma}[The initial value]\label{lem:hyperbinary_zero}
The empty sum is the only hyperbinary representation of $0$, and therefore
$h(0)=1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Odd recurrence]\label{lem:hyperbinary_odd}
For every $n\ge 0$,
\[
  h(2n+1)=h(n).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Even recurrence]\label{lem:hyperbinary_even}
For every $n\ge 1$,
\[
  h(2n)=h(n)+h(n-1).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Consecutive values are coprime]\label{lem:consecutive_coprime}
For every $n\ge 0$,
\[
  \gcd(h(n),h(n+1))=1.
\]
\end{lemma}

\section{Tree Interpretation}

\begin{definition}[Calkin-Wilf children]\label{def:calkin_wilf_children}
For a reduced positive fraction $a/b$, define its two children to be
\[
  \frac{a}{a+b}
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \frac{a+b}{b}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Left child recurrence]\label{lem:left_child_recurrence}
If $q_n=a/b$ in reduced form, then
\[
  q_{2n+1}=\frac{a}{a+b}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Right child recurrence]\label{lem:right_child_recurrence}
If $q_n=a/b$ in reduced form, then
\[
  q_{2n+2}=\frac{a+b}{b}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[The parent step decreases the sum]\label{lem:parent_step_decreases}
Let $a$ and $b$ be coprime positive integers with $(a,b)\ne(1,1)$.  If
$a<b$, then $(a,b-a)$ is a reduced positive fraction and $a+(b-a)<a+b$.
If $b<a$, then $(a-b,b)$ is a reduced positive fraction and $(a-b)+b<a+b$.
\end{lemma}

\section{Main Theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Calkin-Wilf enumeration]\label{thm:calkin_wilf_enumeration}
For every pair of coprime positive integers $a$ and $b$, there exists a unique
integer $n\ge 0$ such that
\[
  h(n)=a
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  h(n+1)=b.
\]
Equivalently, the sequence $q_0,q_1,q_2,\ldots$ contains every positive
rational number exactly once, always in lowest terms.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[An explicit countable listing]\label{cor:explicit_positive_rational_listing}
The function $n\mapsto q_n$ is a bijection from the nonnegative integers to
the positive rational numbers.
\end{corollary}
